newsitem.title: UK: More UK rate hikes needed to curb demand-Barclays.
newsitem.headline: More UK rate hikes needed to curb demand-Barclays.

text.p: The prospect of an increasingly unbalanced economic growth pattern suggests further British interest rate rises are necessary, Barclays Bank economics director Chris Wright said.

In Barclays' third-quarter 1997 Economic Review, Wright said revenue-raising measures falling directly on households are very modest, and domestic demand looks likely to remain sufficiently strong to jeopardise inflation targets two years or so ahead.
"Consumer demand looks set for unsustainably rapid growth, but the high level of sterling has intensified concern that manufacturing industry will be hit.
"On balance the best chance of avoiding a more volatile growth and inflation cycle still seems to be to raise interest rates further," said Wright.
He said recent economic data have been giving mixed signals, particularly those showing a pick-up in underlying retail price inflation despite the strength of the pound.

"At 4.25 percent, the current rate of earnings growth is compatible with achieving the inflation target of 2.5 percent and does not in itself provide the grounds for a further tightening in monetary policy," said Wright.

He said a number of forecasters had emphasised the potential impact on manufacturing industry of sterling's strength, and the tightening of fiscal policy in place. They expect growth to slow quite sharply in the second half of this year and see below-trend growth next year.
But domestic demand has considerable momentum, and lack of action now would risk a more volatile growth and inflation cycle, he said.

"On this view, which we share, the best chance of avoiding such an outcome would be for interest rates to rise to around 8.0 percent by early next year even though it would risk exporters facing very difficult conditions," Wright said.
British base rates were last increased on July 10, to 6.75 percent from 6.50.

Barclays forecasts GDP to average 3.5 percent in 1997, falling to 3.0 percent in 1998. Retail price inflation excluding mortgages is forecast at 2.2 percent by year-end, and 3.2 percent by the end of 1998.
